name: Phrase
tagline: Manage a modest string catalog with review and CI sync

pricing.notes: Pricing is sales-led; canonical monthly amount is null.

tiers.name: Freelancer
tiers.limits: 1 TMS seat; unlimited projects/languages; 650,000 TMS processed words/year; 1,000,000 MTUs/year; 1 Portal user
tiers.notes: Annual billing price; no Strings seats.

tiers.name: Software UI/UX
tiers.limits: 15 Strings seats; 5 Strings projects; 1,000,000 managed words; 500,000 TMS processed words/year; 1,000,000 MTUs/year

tiers.name: Professional
tiers.limits: Unlimited TMS seats/projects/languages; 15 Strings seats; 200,000 Strings managed words; 4,000,000 TMS processed words/year
tiers.notes: Annual billing price; sold under Freelancer & LSP plans.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: Unlimited TMS seats/projects/languages; 20 Strings seats; 1,200,000 managed words; 2,500,000 TMS processed words/year; 12,000,000 MTUs/year

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: 150 Strings seats; unlimited TMS seats/projects/languages; 3,000,000 managed words and 12,000,000 TMS processed words/year on direct-business package

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: 150+ Strings seats and custom product capacities

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; 14-day trial with Enterprise features except integrations that require additional fees
pricing.billingTerms: annual + quarterly; published prices are annual-billing equivalents, quarterly prices require sales contact
pricing.hiddenCosts: Capacity top-ups for seats, processed/managed words, MTUs, AIUs, workflows, models and Portal users are sold separately; Phrase Studio is a volume add-on; professional translation starts at $0.06/word.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Phrase, manage a modest string catalog with review and CI sync. The hard boundary is enterprise translation management, automation, integrations, analytics, and global operations, plus translation memory, collaboration, and deployment integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Manage a modest catalog of translation keys with review and CI sync, preserve context, import and export standard files, and publish approved strings.
requirements: optional DeepL or OpenAI API key
whatYouLose: enterprise translation management, automation, integrations, analytics, and global operations
moatNotes: translation memory, collaboration, and deployment integrations
ongoingBurden: file formats, placeholders, plural rules, screenshots, context, permissions, review, glossary, machine translation, sync, and backups
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Phrase because localization teams pay because language context, review discipline, translators, and release integrations are the hard parts. The recurring cost buys file formats, placeholders, plural rules, screenshots, context, permissions, review, glossary, machine translation, sync, and backups, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Tolgee
priorArt.desc: Active open-source localization platform with translation memory and in-context tooling.

alternatives.name: Tolgee
alternatives.desc: A modest string catalog with review, memory, in-context editing and CI-friendly tooling, without a modest invoice.

facts.install: Hosted Tolgee Cloud signup or the official Docker Compose deployment with PostgreSQL
facts.engines: Tolgee's contextual AI translator and machine-translation layer can connect to Google Cloud Translation, Amazon Translate, DeepL, Microsoft Azure Translator, Baidu, and configured LLM/MT providers.
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted projects, keys, translations, users, and translation memory live in PostgreSQL, while screenshots and uploaded files live under the persistent data directory; cloud accounts store the same classes of data on Tolgee infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: Tolgee covers the catalog but not Phrase's full enterprise suite of orchestration, analytics, mobile delivery, broad connectors, quality management, and service guarantees.
facts.setupBlocker: None for cloud signup; self-hosting needs Docker, an external PostgreSQL database, persistent file storage, mail/domain/TLS, backups, and provider keys for third-party translation engines.

alternatives.name: Weblate
alternatives.desc: Continuous localization tied directly to source control, with mature review and translation-memory workflows.

facts.install: Hosted Weblate signup or the official Docker Compose deployment
facts.engines: Machine translation can connect to OpenAI/Azure OpenAI, DeepL, Google Cloud, Amazon Translate, Microsoft Translator, LibreTranslate, Baidu, Yandex, and other documented services.
facts.dataFormat: Translations, users, review state, memory, glossaries, and settings live in PostgreSQL; cloned source repositories and uploaded files live in persistent server volumes, with Valkey/Redis used for queues and caches.
facts.gapVsPaid: Weblate is less turnkey and lacks Phrase's enterprise orchestration, design and content integrations, OTA/mobile delivery, analytics, and managed-service polish.
facts.setupBlocker: Cloud hosting is free only for qualifying libre projects; the general free route requires Docker, PostgreSQL, Valkey/Redis, domain/TLS, mail, repository credentials, backups, and upgrades.

alternatives.name: Mozilla Pontoon
alternatives.desc: A real TMS for catalog review and repository sync, though deployment assumes an adult is present.

facts.install: Docker setup is documented for development; production deployment must be adapted from Mozilla/Heroku-style infrastructure
facts.dataFormat: Projects sync translations to version-control repositories, while users, suggestions, reviews, translation memory, and job state live in Pontoon's server databases and caches; Mozilla's public instance is not a general hosted service.
facts.gapVsPaid: Pontoon lacks Phrase's supported cloud, workflow orchestration, integration breadth, mobile delivery, analytics, and enterprise administration.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is that the official Docker stack is explicitly not for production and the project does not provide a turnkey supported deployment for arbitrary operators.

alternatives.name: Accent
alternatives.desc: A focused string catalog with collaboration, history and command-line sync; refreshingly uninterested in becoming a platform.

facts.install: Run the published Docker image with an external PostgreSQL database and production environment variables
facts.dataFormat: Projects, languages, strings, translations, comments, history, and users live in PostgreSQL; application configuration and secrets live on the server.
facts.gapVsPaid: Accent is much narrower than Phrase, with no comparable orchestration, translation memory and MT layer, integration catalog, mobile delivery, analytics, or enterprise controls.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is a production Elixir web deployment with Docker, external PostgreSQL, SECRET_KEY_BASE and authentication configuration, TLS, mail, backups, and upgrades; the old standalone Accent CLI is archived.

alternatives.name: Ever Traduora
alternatives.desc: Teams, string search, suggestions, standard imports and exports, and an API in a compact Docker deployment.

facts.install: Official Docker Compose deployment; Kubernetes and source-build paths are also documented
facts.dataFormat: Projects, terms, translations, teams, suggestions, and API credentials live in the configured PostgreSQL/MySQL database, with configuration and logs on the server.
facts.gapVsPaid: Ever Traduora handles a compact string catalog but has much thinner repository sync, translation memory, quality checks, automation, integrations, and enterprise workflow than Phrase.
facts.setupBlocker: A non-expert has to configure Docker, the database, environment secrets and the initial administrator, then add HTTPS, mail, backups, and upgrades.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Team plan and a small-team string-management system DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Phrase in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and one optional machine-translation API; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: manage a modest catalog of translation keys with review and CI sync, preserve context, import and export standard files, and publish approved strings.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement projects, locales, keys, namespaces, descriptions, screenshots, translations, and review status.
Import and export JSON, YAML, PO, and XLIFF while preserving placeholders and plural forms.
Add glossary checks, missing-string filters, translation memory, comments, and reviewer assignment.
Use machine translation only on selected strings and show provider, cost, and source text before approval.
Provide token-authenticated pull and push endpoints for CI with an immutable change log.
Add backups, locale deletion safeguards, and a pseudo-localization preview.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out a translator labor marketplace.
Deliberately leave out a global website translation proxy.
Deliberately leave out enterprise integrations, legal translation assurance, and round-the-clock support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
